title: Playing by ear
summary: Pick out the first four bars of a tune you know, by ear, with no page in front of you.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: Four boxes stacked, standing for the first four bars of a tune you know, found by ear, one key tried at a time, with no page in front of you.

steps.title: Playing by ear
steps.body:
Every piece on the page started as a sound in someone's head before it was written down. This week you work the other way: sound first, page second, or no page at all.

Pick a tune you know well and can hum from memory, not one from your teacher's book.

1. Hum or sing the first four bars softly, on your own.
2. Find the first note on the keyboard by trying a few keys until one matches.
3. Find the next few notes the same way, checking each one against the tune in your head.
4. Play the four bars three times in a row until they come without searching.

This is a different muscle from reading. Reading turns a page into sound. Playing by ear turns a sound already in your head into the right keys, and it gets easier every time you try it.

figure.alt: A one-octave keyboard from middle C, with the A above middle C highlighted as the note played firmly for the tuner or spectrum app, to watch for more than one spike from what feels like a single note.

steps.title: Overtones give a note its colour
steps.body:
A piano key does not make one pure wiggle in the air. It makes a stack: the main wiggle, which sets the pitch, plus faster wiggles layered on top, called overtones. The overtones are why a piano's A and a violin's A can both wiggle 440 times a second and still sound nothing alike.

Predict first: is a single piano note really only one wiggle, or several at once? Write your guess in the Practice log.

Measure: open a free tuner or spectrum app, play one note firmly, and watch the display for more than one spike.

Compare: how many spikes did you see, and were they where you expected?

Teach it: explain to someone why two instruments can play the exact same note and still sound completely different.

figure.alt: Four boxes stacked for the tune's first four bars, played by ear three times in a row until they come without searching for the keys.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: find the first four bars of the tune by ear, no page
Sitting 2: the same four bars, three times without searching
Sitting 3: try the tune starting from a different note, and find it again
Sitting 4: the four bars once through as if recording, then this week's written piece
An old piece played once, from the page

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Say the name of the tune, then play the four bars by ear. Then play this week's written piece once through, hands in the frame.
